lineages.title: The Trumpet
lineages.intro:
Jazz began as a trumpet music: the cornet led the New Orleans band, and Louis Armstrong turned the lead voice into the solo voice. Every trumpeter since has answered him, by adding speed and harmony, as Dizzy Gillespie did, or by taking notes away, as Miles Davis did.

Follow the line and listen for two things: how high and fast each player goes, and how much space they leave.

players.idea: The New Orleans cornet lead, with mutes and plungers that made the horn talk.
Turned the lead line into the solo: swing, the high register and the blues in every phrase.
A cooler, rounder tone and thoughtful phrasing, the other way to play in the 1920s.
The growling plunger trumpet of Ellington's band, then a big open sound of his own.
Bebop's harmony and speed on the trumpet, up into registers no one had used.
Fewer notes, the middle register, the Harmon mute: the trumpet as a voice of understatement.
Bebop with warmth: fat tone, perfect articulation and long, singing lines.
Hard bop swagger: half-valve smears, bluesy cries and a grin in the sound.
Brilliant, brassy power across hard bop, modal jazz and the avant-garde.
Virtuosity in the service of the whole tradition, from New Orleans to Miles.
A bebop trumpeter at home in hip-hop and neo-soul.
Breathy, vocal tone and long silences: the trumpet as a poet's instrument.
players.track: Ambrose Akinmusire|Confessions to My Unborn Daughter

links.note: Armstrong called Oliver his mentor; Oliver sent for him to play second cornet in his Chicago band in 1922.
Williams started out modelling his open horn on Armstrong's, before Ellington made him a growl specialist.
By way of Roy Eldridge, Gillespie came out of Armstrong, and said so: 'No him, no me.'
Miles came to New York in 1944 to find Parker and Gillespie, learned bebop from Dizzy, then went the other way: fewer notes, middle register.
Morgan's early style was built on Brown's; after Brown's death in 1956 he was hailed as his heir.
Hubbard grew up in Indianapolis studying Brown's records, and his bright attack starts there.
Marsalis's early playing with Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers drew on Hubbard, who had held the same chair.
Marsalis's first quintet took Miles Davis's mid-1960s quintet as its model.
Marsalis heard the teenage Hargrove at his Dallas high school in 1987 and helped launch his career.

lineages.title: The Saxophone
lineages.intro:
The saxophone came late to jazz and became its signature sound. Two founding tenors set up the argument everyone since has joined: Coleman Hawkins's big tone and harmonic thinking, and Lester Young's light, floating lines. Charlie Parker joined them on alto and made the saxophone the voice of modern jazz; John Coltrane took it as far as it could go.

Listen for the tone first, heavy or airy, then for how each player handles the chords.

players.idea: The first great saxophone soloist, on soprano, with a wide, operatic vibrato.
The tenor as a solo instrument: a huge tone and solos built on the chords.
A light, airy tone and relaxed, melodic lines that floated over the beat.
The most beautiful alto sound of the swing era, gliding between notes.
Breathy ballads and a growl on the up-tempo numbers.
Bebop itself: speed, new harmony and the blues, on alto.
Bebop on tenor with a big, laid-back sound.
The cool tenor: a pure, singing tone that made bossa nova a hit.
Thematic improvisation: developing a solo from a motif, with wit.
Parker's language with the warmth of the church: soul on alto.
Sheets of sound, then modes, then spiritual search: the saxophone pushed to its limits.
Melody without chord changes: free jazz on a plastic alto.
Wide leaps and bird-like cries on alto, flute and bass clarinet.
The composer's saxophone: elliptical phrases that leave things unsaid.
A personal blend of hard bop, modal and free, with a distinctive cry.
Overblown screams and gentle chants: spiritual jazz on tenor.
players.track: Pharoah Sanders|The Creator Has a Master Plan

players.idea: Free jazz with the blues and the ballad still inside it, and a political edge.
The tradition's language played with clarity and lyricism for a new generation.
Coltrane's and Sanders's spiritual jazz at epic, orchestral scale.
Short, chant-like riffs over Caribbean and African rhythms.
A warm, dark tenor over dub, Afrobeat and London club rhythms.

links.note: Webster's big tone and rhapsodic ballads came out of Hawkins, whom he admired openly.
Rollins grew up idolising Hawkins; in 1963 they recorded together, on Sonny Meets Hawk!
As a teenager in Kansas City, Parker learned Young's solos from Count Basie records note for note.
Getz and the other 'Four Brothers' tenors built their light, airy sound on Young's.
Gordon named Young as his first model, and added bebop to Young's relaxed flow.
When Adderley arrived in New York in 1955, critics called him 'the new Bird'.
Dolphy's alto starts from Parker's language, then stretches its intervals until they break.
Coleman learned Parker's bebop in Texas, then threw away the chord changes it ran on.
Coltrane named Gordon among his early influences; Gordon's bebop tenor was the bridge from Young and Hawkins.
Shorter and Coltrane practised together in the late 1950s; Shorter later held the tenor chair Coltrane had in Miles Davis's quintet.
Henderson absorbed Coltrane's modal and harmonic ideas and found his own sound inside them.
Sanders joined Coltrane's band in 1965 and carried its spiritual search on after Coltrane's death.
Coltrane championed Shepp and helped bring him to Impulse!, which signed him in 1964.
Redman names Coltrane and Rollins, alongside his father Dewey Redman, as his foundations.
Washington's music openly descends from Sanders's spiritual jazz and Coltrane's last bands.

lineages.title: The Piano
lineages.intro:
The piano is the jazz orchestra in one instrument: rhythm in the left hand, melody and harmony in the right. Ragtime wrote it down, stride set it swinging, Art Tatum took it to virtuoso heights, and bebop's pianists turned it into a horn. Then Bill Evans changed its harmony for everyone who followed.

Listen to the left hand: it tells you which generation you're in.

players.idea: Composed ragtime: the left hand's march, the right hand's syncopations, written down.
Ragtime loosened into jazz, with arranged breaks and a Spanish tinge.
Harlem stride: a leaping left hand and a swinging right.
Stride with humour and lightness, and a singer's gift for melody.
'Trumpet-style' piano: right-hand octaves that cut through a band like a horn.
Stride rooted, but the piano as the composer's sketchpad for an orchestra.
Unmatched virtuosity: runs, reharmonisations and speed that stunned other pianists.
Dissonance, space and surprise: every note placed deliberately.
Bebop piano: right-hand horn lines over sparse left-hand chords.
Impressionist voicings without the root and a trio of equals.
Chords built in fourths and a thunderous left hand, the sound of Coltrane's quartet.
Harmonic daring in Miles's quintet, then funk and electronics.
Free piano as percussion: clusters, energy and architecture.
Long improvised solo concerts and the standards trio's singing lines.
Contrapuntal lines in both hands, and pop songs as standards.
players.track: Brad Mehldau|Blame It on My Youth

players.idea: Jazz harmony with hip-hop's beat and R&B's voices.

links.note: Stride grew out of ragtime: Johnson learned the rags before freeing the left hand and loosening the rhythm.
Waller took lessons from Johnson as a teenager in Harlem.
Ellington learned Johnson's Carolina Shout from a piano roll, slowing it down to copy it.
Powell's speed and harmonic reach owed a great deal to Tatum, whom he idolised.
Monk took the teenage Powell under his wing at Minton's and stood up for him.
Evans named Powell among his early models before finding his own harmonic world.
Tyner grew up in Philadelphia with Bud Powell's family in the neighbourhood; Powell was his first model.
Hancock has said that Evans's voicings shaped his own harmony.
Jarrett's ballad touch and trio interplay continue what Evans's trio began.
Mehldau's trio, and his lyrical, introspective playing, are often traced to Evans, as he acknowledges.
Taylor named Ellington, with Monk, as a source for his own wildly different piano.
Glasper cites Hancock as a main influence, and plays his Maiden Voyage alongside Radiohead.

lineages.title: The Bass
lineages.intro:
The bass began as the band's floor: Walter Page's even walking four in the Basie band was the pulse everyone stood on. Jimmy Blanton, in two years with Ellington, showed it could also be a solo voice, and nearly every modern bassist traces back to him. After that the question was how far it could lead: Mingus ran bands from it, Paul Chambers and Ron Carter made the time elastic, Charlie Haden set it free, and Jaco Pastorius made the electric bass sing.

Listen under the soloist: the walking line is a melody of its own, choosing the notes that steer the harmony.

players.idea: The walking four of the Basie rhythm section: even, light and unstoppable.
The bass as a solo voice: horn-like lines, a huge tone, and the bow.
Led the band from the bass, driving, shouting and composing as he played.
A classical player's range and an unpredictable swing for the avant-garde.
The hard-bop pulse: buoyant walking lines and bowed solos taken seriously.
Elastic, conversational time, from Albert Ayler's free jazz to Jarrett's standards.
A deep, singing tone and harmonic choices that let the bass steer the band.
Few notes, each one chosen: a folk-deep bass that moved with the soloist.
The fretless electric bass as a lead voice: melodies, chords and harmonics.
Sings over her own bass lines, in songs that range from jazz to art-pop.

links.note: Blanton's solos with Ellington inspired Mingus to raise the bass up from the rhythm section into the lead.
Blanton was Chambers's all-time favourite bassist, Leonard Feather wrote; his bowed solos carry Blanton's arco on.
Chambers admired Mingus for broadening the scope of jazz bass, and drew on him alongside Pettiford and Heath.
Davis says it was Blanton's sound on Ellington's records that drew him to the bass.
Haden said he loved Blanton, one of the first bass players he remembered listening to.
Haden called Chambers the first bassist who was really distinctive to him: the chromatic lines, the sound, the time.
Peacock's playing came out of Paul Chambers, with Ray Brown and Scott LaFaro.
Jaco named Carter among the bassists he dug coming up, with Jerry Jemmott and Gary Peacock.
Peacock was on Jaco's own list of the players he dug coming up, next to Ron Carter.
Spalding has named Carter, with Dave Holland, as an important influence on her music.

lineages.title: The Drums
lineages.intro:
Jazz drumming moved the time from the bass drum to the cymbals, and the drummer from timekeeper to conversation partner. Kenny Clarke started it in the bebop years; Max Roach made the kit melodic; Elvin Jones and Tony Williams made it the centre of the band.

Listen to the ride cymbal: it's where the time lives.

players.idea: New Orleans drumming: press rolls and constant colour on a small kit.
Moved the time to the ride cymbal and 'dropped bombs' on the bass drum.
Melodic drumming: solos built like compositions, and a crisp, driving ride.
Press rolls, shuffle grooves and thunder behind the soloists.
Crisp, unpredictable snare comments; 'snap crackle'.
Polyrhythm: triplets rolling over the beat, the drums as a churning sea.
A smiling, light ride cymbal that made free and hard bop both swing.
Time that stretched and broke, at seventeen, in Miles's quintet; then fusion's power.
Fluid, colouristic time across the standards trio and fusion.
players.track: Keith Jarrett, Gary Peacock & Jack DeJohnette|God Bless the Child

players.idea: Live drumming edited like a beat-maker: jazz built from loops.

links.note: Roach built on Clarke's innovations, the ride-cymbal time and bass-drum accents, and said so.
Williams studied Roach's playing as a boy in Boston; Roach was his model before Miles hired him.
DeJohnette names Jones as a major influence; the rolling, polyrhythmic feel carries straight over.

lineages.title: The Guitar
lineages.intro:
The guitar came into jazz as a rhythm instrument, strumming four to the bar and too quiet to solo over a band; Freddie Green kept it that way in the Basie band for fifty years. Django Reinhardt made it a solo voice in Paris, amplification let it stand up to the horns, and from there it went into the organ trios, bossa nova and fusion's volume.

Listen for single lines played like a horn, and for the chords underneath when the guitar comps.

players.idea: Gypsy jazz: blazing runs from a burned hand, and Europe's first great jazz voice.
Rhythm guitar as the band's heartbeat: even, chunky chords, four to the bar.
Warm, blues-soaked and unhurried: the sound of soul-jazz guitar.
players.track: Kenny Burrell|Back at the Chicken Shack

players.idea: The bossa nova guitar: samba distilled into a soft, offbeat pulse under the voice.
Clean, horn-like single lines steeped in the blues, from organ grooves to modal dates.
Fusion's lightning: rock volume, Indian rhythm and jazz harmony at full speed.
A warm, singing tone and wide-open melodies, from trio to cinematic group music.

links.note: Burrell said Django showed him that you could find your own individuality on the instrument.
McLaughlin heard Django at about fourteen; he and Tal Farlow were his heroes on guitar, he said, and still are.
Metheny calls Burrell one of his main heroes, for his sound, his touch and his natural blues phrasing.

lineages.title: The Voice
lineages.intro:
Jazz singing began with the blues queens of the 1920s, who sang over jazz bands in vaudeville tents. Louis Armstrong showed that a singer could improvise like a horn; Billie Holiday turned that into intimacy; Ella Fitzgerald and Sarah Vaughan into virtuosity. Every singer since has drawn on those few.

Listen for where the singer sits against the beat, and how far they'll bend the melody.

players.idea: The Mother of the Blues: a huge, earthy voice from the tent shows.
The Empress of the Blues: power and control, every word weighed.
Sang like he played: rewriting melodies, swinging the words, inventing scat on record.
Behind the beat and inside the lyric: phrasing as storytelling.
Perfect pitch, joyful swing and the greatest scat singing on record.
An operatic range and bebop harmony in the voice.
Classical piano, gospel and protest in one voice.
players.track: Nina Simone|My Baby Just Cares for Me

players.idea: A dark contralto taking the blues, folk and pop into jazz.
players.track: Cassandra Wilson|You Don't Know What Love Is

players.idea: Theatrical, witty and precise, from 1920s blues to new songs.

links.note: The two toured in the same travelling shows around 1912, and Rainey is often said to have coached the young Smith.
Holiday said she learned to sing from Bessie Smith's and Louis Armstrong's records.
Holiday wanted Armstrong's feeling in her voice: his phrasing, not his sound, she said.
McLorin Salvant names Vaughan, with Bessie Smith and Billie Holiday, among the singers she studied.
Her repertoire reaches back to 1920s blues and vaudeville, songs Bessie Smith sang.

lineages.title: The Trombone
lineages.intro:
In the New Orleans band the trombone played underneath: Kid Ory filled the gaps below the cornet with slides and smears, a style called tailgate. The swing era made it a soloist, smooth and singing in Jack Teagarden's hands, talkative and full of tricks in Dicky Wells's. Bebop was harder, because a slide is slow for fast lines; J.J. Johnson's answer, clean tonguing that made the trombone sound almost like a valve instrument, became the model most modern players followed, and the rest defined themselves against it.

Listen for the slide: how much each player smears between notes, and how much they hide it.

players.idea: Tailgate trombone: rhythmic slides and smears under the cornet, the New Orleans band's bass line in brass.
The trombone as a blues singer: long, smooth lines with the slide almost hidden.
A talking trombone: rips, slurs and growls placed with a comedian's timing in Count Basie's band.
Bebop on the trombone: clean, tongued notes at speed, so the slide sounded like valves.
Charlie Parker's lines on the slide, smooth and unpredictable, in Mingus's bands.
A warm, round hard-bop sound, with Art Blakey's Messengers and on Coltrane's Blue Train.

links.note: Teagarden never played the tailgate style Ory had made the trombone's job; he played long, smooth solos the way a trumpeter would.
Wells and Trummy Young were the first trombonists Johnson admired; he loved Wells's playing, he said, for its minimum of articulation.
As a boy in a Detroit orphanage, Fuller was taken to hear Illinois Jacquet's band with Johnson on trombone; Johnson became his main model.
Knepper said most modern trombonists imitated J.J.; his own influences weren't trombonists at all, but Charlie Parker, whose solos he transcribed.

lineages.title: The Clarinet
lineages.intro:
The clarinet was the New Orleans band's high voice, weaving around the cornet's melody. Johnny Dodds and Sidney Bechet both took lessons from the Creole Tio family of clarinetists, and the records the New Orleans players made in Chicago in the 1920s reached a teenage Benny Goodman there. In the swing era the clarinet led the most popular bands in America; after bebop it moved to the edges, where Eric Dolphy made the bass clarinet a solo voice and Anat Cohen made the clarinet sound new again.

Listen for the tone, dark and woody low down, bright and piercing at the top, and then for the vibrato: wide and fast in New Orleans, narrower or gone later.

players.idea: The New Orleans blues clarinet: a big, dark tone and crying phrases in Oliver's and Armstrong's bands.
A clarinetist before he was a saxophonist: a huge tone and a wide, fast vibrato that led any band he was in.
Swing's clarinet: a clean, centred tone and fast, even runs, in front of a big band and in small groups.
A clarinetist with a composer's ambitions: a pure, soaring top register, strings, and a concerto of his own.
Made the bass clarinet a solo instrument: honks, cries and wide leaps across its whole range.
The bass clarinet as atmosphere: dark, slow-moving lines inside the electric bands of Miles Davis and Herbie Hancock.
A warm, singing clarinet at home in New Orleans jazz, Brazilian choro and modern small groups.

links.note: Goodman grew up in Chicago listening to its New Orleans clarinetists, Dodds among them, and said no one ever surpassed Dodds's tone.
Rivals at the top of swing with different aims: Shaw recalled telling Goodman he was too hung up on the clarinet, while Shaw was trying to play music.
Cohen started on clarinet in a Dixieland band in Tel Aviv, and names Bechet, with John Coltrane, as her two great heroes growing up.
Goodman was Cohen's first introduction to jazz clarinet; for his centenary she played his repertoire in her Clarinetwork band at the Village Vanguard.
Maupin heard Dolphy and met him in Detroit, where Dolphy gave him a flute lesson; Dolphy's bass clarinet showed him what the instrument could do.

lineages.title: The Vibraphone
lineages.intro:
The vibraphone was a 1920s novelty, metal bars over tubes with a motor that makes the sound pulse. Red Norvo had already shown on xylophone and marimba how quietly a mallet instrument could swing; Lionel Hampton, a drummer, made the vibes a jazz voice in Benny Goodman's quartet. Milt Jackson slowed the pulse down and played bebop and the blues on it, and nearly every vibraphonist since comes from him or from Gary Burton, who played it like a piano with four mallets.

Listen for the shimmer, how long each player lets notes ring, and count the mallets: two for horn-like lines, four for chords.

players.idea: Chamber jazz on mallets: a light, quiet touch on xylophone and marimba, then a trio with guitar and bass instead of drums.
Made the vibraphone a jazz instrument: a drummer's drive, hard riffs and swing in the Goodman Quartet.
Bebop and the blues on vibes: a slow, warm vibrato and long, singing lines.
Brought the vibes into Latin jazz: cool, clear lines over Cuban rhythm.
Open, ringing chords and fast, modern lines: the vibes in Blue Note's 1960s avant-garde.
Four mallets and piano voicings: the vibraphone as a full harmony instrument, in duets and country-tinged jazz.
Two mallets, little pedal, and a band that talks across different pulses.

links.note: Jackson took up the vibraphone at sixteen after hearing Hampton with Benny Goodman's band.
Tjader named Hampton as his first inspiration on vibes, before Milt Jackson became his model.
Tjader said Jackson influenced him strongly; his cool, bluesy lines on the Latin dates come from Bags.
As a boy Hutcherson heard Jackson play Bemsha Swing on a Miles Davis record and decided to take up the vibraphone.
Burton called Norvo his great example; on his 2001 tribute For Hamp, Red, Bags, and Cal he re-created Norvo's 1950s trio.
Ross grew up on Jackson's records and names him as his formative influence on the instrument; like Jackson, he plays with two mallets.
At eighteen Ross visited Hutcherson at home in California; Hutcherson told him to write about his own life, advice Ross says he took literally.

lineages.title: The Organ
lineages.intro:
Fats Waller recorded jazz on the pipe organ in the 1920s, but the Hammond became a jazz instrument of its own in the 1950s. Wild Bill Davis led some of the first organ trios, with guitar and drums; Jimmy Smith played the Hammond with a bebop horn player's speed, the bass line on the lower keyboard, and the organ trio became the sound of soul jazz. Larry Young took it into Coltrane's modal world and fusion, and Joey DeFrancesco brought it back to the centre of jazz at the end of the 1980s.

Listen to the left hand and the pedals: they play the bass, so the organist is half the rhythm section too. Then listen for the drawbars and the rotating speaker, which make the sound swell and whirl.

players.idea: Jazz on the pipe organ in the 1920s and on the Hammond in 1942, with stride's bounce in both.
An early Hammond trio leader, with guitar and drums, who gave the organ the punch of a big band.
Made the Hammond B-3 a jazz instrument: bebop speed in the right hand, walking bass in the left, the blues all through.
Soul jazz with a light, crisp touch, trading choruses with tenor saxophonists.
The blues and gospel organ: a big, churchy sound and grooves built for dancing.
Took the organ into Coltrane's modal world, then fusion: open chords and long, floating lines.
Church organ and funk: slow-building grooves, swelling chords and the Hammond's wildest sounds.
Brought the organ back to jazz in the late 1980s, playing Jimmy Smith's language at a blazing pace.

links.note: Davis took Waller and Art Tatum as his early models, before he moved from piano and guitar to the organ.
Smith switched from piano to organ for good in 1954 after hearing Davis play.
Lonnie Smith remembered hearing Davis on the radio first, then Jimmy Smith; he learned from Davis's records and from the church organ.
After Davis came Jimmy Smith's records, which Lonnie Smith immersed himself in as a young player in Buffalo.
Scott said Jackie Davis and Jimmy Smith were the first two organists who inspired her to take up the instrument.
Smith was a childhood friend; McGriff took private lessons from him, and from Milt Buckner, after buying his first Hammond in 1956.
Young's first records were soul jazz in Smith's manner; at Blue Note from 1964 he turned toward Coltrane.
DeFrancesco was playing Smith's records note for note at five; Smith became his mentor and recorded with him on Incredible! and Legacy.
